theme: Judgment on the nations; the LORD dwells in Zion
readingInstruction: Read Joel 3:1-21 (in some Bibles, Joel 2:28-3:21). The LORD gathers the nations for judgment, and the book ends with a vision of a fountain from the LORD’s house. Read it as the final answer to the locusts.
settingTheScene: Joel’s last chapter looks forward to the final day. The LORD will judge the nations for how they treated his people, and his own people will dwell in safety. The language is vivid, with images of a valley of decision and a fountain flowing from the temple. It points past the post-exilic community to the end of history.
observation: “For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem” (3:1).
“I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat” (3:2).
“Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears” (3:10).
“Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision! For the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision” (3:14).
“The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining” (3:15).
“But the LORD is a refuge to his people, a stronghold to the people of Israel” (3:16).
“So you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who dwells in Zion, my holy mountain” (3:17).
“And a fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD and water the Valley of Shittim” (3:18).
interpretation:
Joel moves from the locusts to the end of the world. God promises to “restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,” language like Psalm 126. Then he will gather the nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, a name meaning “the LORD judges.” There he will judge them for scattering his people and dividing the land, and for selling the children of Israel as slaves.

This section is hard to read, because it describes judgment. But it contains a fundamental truth. God sees injustice and will set it right. For those who are oppressed, this is good news. The prayer for justice is answered. The line “Beat your plowshares into swords” is an inversion of the later promise in Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, where swords are beaten into plowshares. Here, the nations are summoned to war and are met by God.

The “valley of decision” is the place where judgment is decided. The phrase can mean the decision God makes, not our decision. Still, the image captures the seriousness of the moment. Everyone will stand before the Judge. The sun and moon darken, and the LORD roars from Zion. Yet “the LORD is a refuge to his people, a stronghold to the people of Israel.” The same event that terrifies his enemies shelters his people.

The book ends with restoration. The mountains drip sweet wine, the hills flow with milk, and the streambeds run with water. A fountain flows from the house of the LORD. Egypt and Edom will be desolate, but Judah will be inhabited forever. “The LORD dwells in Zion.” That final sentence is the book’s answer to the locusts. The land will be restored, and God will be with his people.

The fountain from the temple is a thread through the whole Bible, from Eden’s river to Ezekiel 47 to Revelation 22.
connection: Revelation 22:1-2 shows the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. John 7:37-38: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 invert the swords and plowshares. Matthew 25:31-46 describes the judgment of the nations. Revelation 14:14-20 uses the harvest image from Joel 3:13. Romans 12:19: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”
application:
Pray for those who suffer injustice, trusting God to judge rightly.

Remember that the same day that is terrifying to enemies is a refuge for those who trust in the LORD.

Drink from the fountain: spend time in worship, asking Christ to satisfy your thirst.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he judges rightly and is a refuge to his people.
Ask him to make you ready for his day.
Ask him to let his fountain flow from his house.
